title: How to Read a Cannabis Label, Line by Line | CastleLeaf
h1: How to Read a Cannabis Label, Line by Line
description: Percentages, milligrams, ratios and batch numbers: a step by step guide to reading a cannabis label, so you know what is in the package before you open it.
excerpt: A cannabis label packs a lot into a small space. Here’s how to read one from top to bottom, and which numbers matter most for flower, edibles and concentrates.
pull: Once you know where to look, it reads like a recipe card.

blocks.html: A cannabis label can look like a page from a chemistry textbook squeezed onto a sticker. Take a breath. Once you know where to look, it reads like a recipe card. It tells you more about a product than any name or nickname ever could.
Layouts vary from brand to brand, but most labels cover the same ground. Here’s how we’d read one, top to bottom.

items.title: Product name and type
items.text: What it is (flower, pre-roll, vape, edible, tincture or concentrate) and its cultivar or flavor. The type tells you how the numbers below will be written.

items.title: Cannabinoid content
items.text: How much THC and CBD the product holds, plus any minor cannabinoids. Look for total THC, which also counts the THCA that becomes THC when heated.

items.title: Serving information
items.text: For edibles and tinctures: milligrams per serving, servings per package and the total for the whole package.

items.title: Terpenes
items.text: Many products list their leading terpenes, sometimes with percentages. Think of it as a preview of aroma and flavor.

items.title: Ingredients
items.text: Especially on edibles. Check for allergens the way you would with any food.

items.title: Dates and batch number
items.text: A packaging or harvest date speaks to freshness, and the batch or lot number connects the product to its testing.

items.title: Warnings
items.text: Read them every time, even on a product you know well.

blocks.html: This one trips up a lot of people. Flower, pre-rolls, vapes and concentrates usually list cannabinoids as a percentage of weight. Edibles and tinctures usually list milligrams.

items: Percentages describe concentration. A flower labeled 20% THC holds about 200 mg of THC in every gram, although how much you actually take in depends on how you consume it.
Milligrams describe an amount. A piece labeled 5 mg THC holds 5 mg of THC, which is why edibles are so much easier to measure.
Ratios describe a balance. A product marked 1:1 holds equal amounts of two cannabinoids, usually THC and CBD. Check which one is named first.

blocks.html: Concentrates are, as the name suggests, concentrated, so their percentages run far higher than flower’s. A small amount goes a long way.

In Massachusetts, edibles are capped at 5 mg of THC a serving and 100 mg a package, so a 100 mg package of 5 mg servings holds twenty of them. When you shop, anyone 21+ with a valid government ID can buy up to 1 oz (28 grams) of flower equivalent per day and no more than 5 grams of concentrates.
Our FAQ covers the rest of the basics, from ID to where you can consume.

sections.heading: When the label raises a question

blocks.html: Labels are good at facts and less good at context. They can tell you how much THC a flower holds, but not whether it suits a quiet Sunday with a sketchbook. That’s where people come in.

Bring your questions to the counter. Our budtenders are happy to read a label with you and explain what each number means for the way you like to enjoy cannabis. You belong here, whether it’s your first label or your five hundredth.

faq.a_html: It’s the THC a product will hold once heated: the THC already present plus the THC its THCA will become. On flower, it’s the number to compare.

faq.q: Why do edibles use milligrams and flower use percentages?
faq.a_html: Edibles come in measured servings, so milligrams tell you exactly what’s in each piece. Flower is used in varying amounts, so a percentage of weight is the clearer way to describe its strength.

faq.q: What is the batch number for?
faq.a_html: It ties the product to a specific production run and its testing. Keep the packaging until you’ve finished the product, in case a question comes up later.
